question: to the Commission Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In its reply to my Question E-000527/20261 of 9 February 2026, the Commission explicitly stated on 14 April 2026 that it firmly rejects the unfounded and unsubstantiated allegations set out in the report of the US House Judiciary Committee of 3 February 2026, including those relating to the 2023 Slovak elections. The Commission thus clearly stated that it considers these allegations to be untrue and strongly distances itself from them. 1.

I assume that, since the publication of the US report up to the present day, the Commission has already taken specific diplomatic, political and legal steps to actively safeguard the integrity of its actions and public trust; if not, why not?

Has the Commission formally approached-by diplomatic note, official letter or other official means-the United States House Judiciary Committee, its Chair, or the US Congress with a request for a public correction, retraction, or withdrawal of the false allegations concerning interference in the Slovak elections?

Beyond the brief response to my written question, what other public steps (press releases, statements, media briefings or other forms of communication) has the Commission taken vis-à-vis the European public to actively refute these allegations and defend its credibility?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-000527_EN.html.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission has repeatedly clarified its position to the US administration and the House Judiciary Committee and stands firm on its position that the latter’s Report1 of 3 February 2026 misrepresents the nature of the EU Digital Rulebook. As affirmed by the Spokespersons’ Service at the Midday press briefing on 3 February 2026, the Commission rebuts any allegation that the Digital Rulebook weakens freedom of expression. As indicated in the answer to written question E-000527/20262, freedom of expression is at the heart of the Digital Services Act (DSA3). The DSA helps protect it by giving users the right to explanations, appeals and redress when their content is removed or restricted by platforms. The Commission pursues maximum transparency in its enforcement of the DSA. All enforcement decisions are taken in an open and transparent manner and are published on a dedicated website4. The Commission engages continuously with US representatives at both political and technical level on a wide range of subjects including the EU digital rules with the objective of promoting cooperation to address shared challenges which the online world poses. Enforcing democratically adopted legislation is not up for discussion. This remains the sovereign right of the EU, and the Commission will continue to enforce the DSA fairly, in line with due process and in maximum transparency.
